title: Anthology Botanica
content:
***Pollen Park***
The scent of bush draws me in
Sweet and soft to the nose, the gumnut blossoms
Leaves pepper the ground with colour
Birds sing to one another in the trees
Oh, breathe deeply
Drown in the scent of fresh air
Let it fill your lungs
Breathe out –
Air harvested by trees — a gift
They work even now, surrounding me with their
Towering presence
I am small
I breathe deep
I am small.

***Ants***
Ants dance on the table
Honey coloured bums shaking like maracas
They hunt, for what I cannot see —
Although they could be searching
for treasure unknown,
Unbecoming to me.
The ancients ate them for their sweetness
But I –
I watch them

***Green Gum***
Little tree that towers to the clouds;
tethered to the earth by vine and roots.
Stretch, stretch — ever higher.
Green wood enrobed in bark splintering
are you sick? tired of being tethered to the ground.
I too long to climb higher…

title: Crustlesalt
preview: The story of Crustlesalt the dwarf
content:
In an age, long before anyone living could remember, there roamed the Sons and Daughters of Earth; these were the race of Dwarves, the ancient ones of this world. To the East of this great land were the Crustle Shores.

The waves licked the shoreline, tasting the grit of the sand. This is the kind of gritty sand that gets in your toes. Gritty sea salt and sand. The beach stretched wide, the waves lapping like a tongue, delicately against the shore, white foam frothing on the sand. The sun was high, heat bearing down. The forehead of the Dwarf called Crustlesalt ran with sweat. His eyes looked out onto the waters, his eyes were watchful of the horizon, as if waiting for a friend, his eyes were blue like the sea. With toes covered in sandy salt and salty sand, and the noise of waves delicately lapping against the shoreline, Crustlesalt waited. In impatience, he burrowed his toes into the sand like a mole hiding from the light. The waves rolled in hungrily again.

A call came from out on the waters, and a stirring in the deep. The movement neared the shoreline, and a head popped out from the water to be greeted by the smile of the old Dwarf. A Sea Serpent with a blue hue emerged from the depths, a single horn atop its head, its body sleek, flippers protruding from its sides, its tail slightly transparent. The waves danced excitedly against the shore, as if awakened by the beast.

The Sea Serpent let out a cry, one that echoed out, one so soft and sweet you'd have thought it came from the morning song of the birds of Thicketberry Forest. Old Crustlesalt walked to the Serpent and rested his hand upon the beast's snout.

"It's so very nice to see you, old friend," said the kind voice of Crustlesalt. They stayed like that for some time, before he bent to the ground and sat on the sand.

"I'm afraid there is trouble," his voice now frail. "Dwarves from the mountains have come to the Mangroves. They're suffering."

The Sea Serpent called out loudly, letting it echo around the beach. Storm clouds gathered on the horizon and the waves grew higher and higher. It wasn't longer before the rains came, but the Serpent and the Dwarf were long gone, racing toward the Groves.

Crustlesalt rode on the back of the Sea Serpent, their charge through the waters looked like a hurricane, their faces grave and contemplative.

"We haven't a moment to lose," thought the old Dwarf.

Nearer the shores of the Groves, when Crustlesalt and the Sea Serpent had arrived, they saw the billowing smoke rising from within the forest. The beast called out, deeper and mightier than before, letting all know of their presence. Crustlesalt brandished his axe, carved intricately along the driftwood handle, a shard of stone as its head.

Crustlesalt sprang from the back of the beast into the waters, with surprising agility for his age, and swam quickly toward the shores. His body moved gracefully in the waters, his arms outstretched, swimming below the surface and into the streams of the Mangroves. The old Dwarf made his way through the maze of tangled roots and seaweed, swimming past the many fish that had come to make this their home.

Crustlesalt arose from the waters, walking carefully out into the mysterious forest. He saw dwarves in the distance, covered in soot from the burning of trees, wielding axes against more, felling them to be burned with the rest.

Crustlesalt looked on in anguish. The ancient trees, that had stood here since the Creation itself, were falling to the dwarves of the mountains. Those dwarves whose hearts had turned dark to the likeness of the caves they dwelt in. Then he saw him.

"Cobblestomp!" roared Crustlesalt. "I charge you, in the name of He who gave you breath, with treason against the Creation."

The dwarf called Cobblestomp looked up from his work.

"Crustlesalt," he smirked as he spoke. "My father made an oath, not me."

"Don't speak to me of the oath," Crustlesalt spat. He raised his hands to the skies, with his axe in one, and the sound of the Sea Serpent rang out in power and ferocity, "I was there!"

The dwarves trembled as the skies turned dark, rain pouring from the Heavens, extinguishing their fires. The Sea Serpent arose from the depths, the two companions next one another, facing their opponents fiercely.

title: The Five Sons of Earth
preview: In an age, long before anyone living could remember, there roamed the Sons and Daughters of Earth; these were the race of Dwarves, the ancient ones of this world.
content:
In an age, long before anyone living could remember, there roamed the Sons and Daughters of Earth; these were the race of Dwarves, the ancient ones of this world. Hidden in the mountains, to the north of the world, shrouded by trees of sunset; stood the Dwarvish Kingdom of Mapletop. Those ancient halls, echoed the story of those first formed from the dirt; who've breathed, and grown, and lived. The Mapletop Range spanned much of the northern world, bridging the Maple Woods from the Great Desert. Gold, orange and red sprawled the ground, to the likeness of sunset, all the way up to the great oaken doors of the Kingdom. There, barred by heavy door, was the wealthiest mine of Maplestone throughout the world. Maplestone, an amber coloured gem, lined the walls of the mines deep to the heart of the mountain. Corralled by gems of all colours and sizes, Maplestone was by far the most valuable; its amber glow, the likeness of a flame, could be rivalled by none. It is in these mines that we meet a most peculiar Dwarf, one whose thumbs were green, and heart was as warm as Maplestone.

Warm sunshine spilled out upon the peak of the mountains, bathing the rocky landscape in a warm orangey glow. On a boulder, sat a Dwarf. His legs carelessly hung over the cliff face below as he whistled with the early morning breeze. His face was dark, his age extenuated by the soot that rested within the creases in his skin. He'd breathe in the gentle morning breeze, letting the youthful world grant him rest, as if it gave of its own youthfulness to its people.

I think it best to give Eurkhart himself some description; Eurkhart Barksap was a miner of Mapletop, exceptionally nimble-fingered and light-hearted. Barksap loved to dance to the earthy music of his people, and the feel of the earth on his scarred, worn hands. He was a miner by trade, but his heart would lead him to the plants and animals surrounding his mountain home. Eurkhart looked out on the land, remembering the stories of his grandfather, Eurion Barksap, the stories that told the legends of creation. Eurion was one of the first formed from the dirt, who'd risen from the ground and felt HIS warm breath. For this reason, Eurkhart had always craved the feeling of the dancing breath of the wind on the mountaintop, even to his old age, where legs and back would bend beneath the weight of the climb. His pursed lips would send out sweet music to the clouds, as his hands gripped the solid rock beneath him.

Each day began just like this, and then he'd take to the mines, harvesting the precious gems that grew like flowers throughout the mountain core. Eurkhart was gentle, prying the gems from their home with a tenderness the other Dwarves knew not. Lowered into the depths by ropes, the miners would swing about, from wall to wall, as they worked the gems into their bags. Lunch was Eleven Forty-Five, and not a moment sooner or later.

Eurkhart would break, leaning against the smooth cut walls of the cavern. He'd take out a handkerchief from his pocket, unwrap it delicately, and then pop berries into his mouth. These berries, of course, were much different to any you and I would know. These berries hailed from the very edges of the Maplewood, those trees that were kissed by the sea. It was here that old Eurion was said to have risen from the soil. The berries tasted of maple sap and salty spray, and were Eurkhart's favourite snack.

He'd forage for them each day, on his late afternoon stroll through the woods. On this particular afternoon, the wind howled on the shore, waves breaking against the black craggy rock, spraying sea water over the edge of the Maplewood. Sunlight streamed from west, as Barksap walked along the edge, singing a song of the ancients:

***"Wind blown into dust
Dwarvish folk from the ground came
Working against their tools a rust
To mine the mountains and tether the earth"***

The wind wisped around him, then suddenly came down in a gale, causing him to fall on his face. When Eurkhart looked up, he saw the brightest light he'd ever seen; brighter than even the Sterrastone of the deep mines (that is pure starlight, fallen from the skies long before the first Dwarf). A voice spoke to him, one as powerful as the roaring waves of the shore.

"Take back your roots. Find Cherrystone," said the voice. Eurkhart trembled, and caught his breath.

"Here I am, I will go," he replied.

The light dissipated, and Eurkhart felt his strength return to him. He stood, and walked to the shrubs along the shoreline. He plucked as many berries as he could hold and then walked back to the mountain. That night he packed a sack with as much food as he could carry, and then slept until the early hours of the morning.

The dawn creaked over the mountainside, orange light breaking the horizon. Eurkhart woke, and made his way quietly, keeping out of sight, and leaving through the great oak doors. He slung his sack over his shoulder, lit his pipe, and begin to hum softly to himself. Eurkhart's journey had begun, and even he did not know his destination. He made his way south, over the mountains, and eventually into the dessert. The mountains had proven, familiar, yet formidable. He'd stumbled across the harsh inclining terrain, and was now graced with an endless expanse of yellow sea that stretched on beyond the horizon.

The wind whipped up a sandy breeze against the aged face, stinging his skin. He looked out wistfully on the Great Desert.

"Old friend, I will meet you soon," he whispered into the wind.

Barksap began his journey in the blistering sun, trudging through the ever-unstable sand. His brow was sweaty, and his limbs grew tired. Cactuses lined his path, a mirage of green that fooled his eyes with dreams of oasis. The journey was one of testing, and doubts began to grow in the old Barksap's mind. The comfort of his mountaintop gaze, the afternoon light of his walks in the woods, the spray of the sea. The orange hue of the sun turned deep red, and Eurkhart slumped against a rock, and taking out his water pouch he began to drink. He then carefully took out his handkerchief and delicately unwrapped his berries. He took only four, closing his eyes and savouring the sweet refreshing flavour on his tongue. Then, sleep called his name.

A dream came to him in his sleep, he found himself standing in the desert, and in the middle, was a tree. Upon the tree were lights. Moving lights, to the likeness of that which he had never seen in the Maplewood. Upon the top of the tree stood HE.

"Go, Son of Earth. Take back your roots. Find Cherrystone and remember," said the strong, clear voice.

Eurkhart awoke, seeing first light just breaking the horizon. He lit a small fire, and began to make some breakfast; he took out bread, cured meats and dried fruit. He thought on his dream, and pulled out an aged parchment. He carefully unrolled it, and traced his finger lightly to the desert etched upon it. His finger lightly danced south of the desert finding the ancient Thicketberry Forest, which stretched out upon the entirety of the Southern Coast. He filled up on his breakfast as he investigated the map, the occasional fruit pieces and crumbs falling onto it.

He readied himself, put out the fire, gathered his things and began his journey once again. He trekked through the dessert for a week, his water grew low and his legs tired. Until on the seventh day, he found a stream at last. He replenished his water, and gathered from the mosses what he could to eat. Then he rested. From there he followed the stream south, eventually making his way to the throng of the forest. Thicketberry Forest stood in all its resplendence before him, a vast expanse of green caught by the light of the sun.

"Finally," fell from his breath as he looked out into the forest.

Eurkhart sat, shrouded by leaves in the wooden lodging. Shrubs pocketed their way through the trees, berries of reds and purples wove about the foliage in various clumps and sizes. His hands lay around a rustic wooden mug, with steam gently wafting out of the top as tea was slowly poured in. Before him, stood a creature with flowing brown robes. In his hands lay a teapot, similarly carved from wood as the mug. His eyes gleamed green beneath the wisps of white hair that fell about his face, and a white beard danced about his belly as he moved. His brown robes were covered in moss and vines, and his smile seemed mischievous and kind all at once.

"There were five Sons of Earth, Eurkhart. Your grandfather was one. Duneburnt of the Great Dessert, Crustlesalt of the Eastern Sea, Cobblestone of the Mountains, and myself. We all were the original protectors of our lands, to pass through our generations when our time came," said Cherrystone. He handed Eurkhart a small ring, carved of maple wood.

"This was your grandfather's, but I believe it now belongs to you," his voice shaking as he spoke.

Eurkhart looked up from his tea, his eyes shining with tears and joy.
